**This vehicle answered one question and its first flight was destroyed by another, and both
questions were the same question.** A scramjet's useful output is the difference between the thrust it
makes and the drag it suffers, and each of those is far larger than the difference. A launch vehicle's
stability is the difference between the gain its control loop has and the gain at which it goes
unstable, and each of those is far larger than the difference. **The Hyper-X programme measured the
first correctly and got the second wrong**, and this article treats those as one subject rather than
two.
This is the forty-fourth article in the [X-Planes series][related_post_a297_framing], following the [X-1][related_post_a298_bell_x1], the [X-2][related_post_a299_bell_x2], the [X-3][related_post_a300_douglas_x3], the [X-4][related_post_a301_northrop_x4], the [X-5][related_post_a302_bell_x5], the [X-6][related_post_a303_convair_x6], the [X-7][related_post_a304_lockheed_x7], the [X-8][related_post_a305_aerojet_x8], the [X-9][related_post_a306_bell_x9], the [X-10][related_post_a307_north_american_x10], the [X-11][related_post_a308_convair_x11], the [X-12][related_post_a309_convair_x12], the [X-13][related_post_a310_ryan_x13], the [X-14][related_post_a311_bell_x14], the [X-15][related_post_a312_north_american_x15], the [X-16][related_post_a313_bell_x16], the [X-17][related_post_a314_lockheed_x17], the [X-18][related_post_a315_hiller_x18], the [X-19][related_post_a316_curtiss_wright_x19], the [X-20][related_post_a317_boeing_x20], the [X-21][related_post_a318_northrop_x21], the [X-22][related_post_a319_bell_x22], the [X-23][related_post_a320_martin_marietta_x23], the [X-24][related_post_a321_martin_marietta_x24], the [X-25][related_post_a322_bensen_x25], the [X-26][related_post_a323_schweizer_x26], the [X-27][related_post_a324_lockheed_x27], the [X-28][related_post_a325_osprey_x28], the [X-29][related_post_a326_grumman_x29], the [X-30][related_post_a327_rockwell_x30], the [X-31][related_post_a328_rockwell_mbb_x31], the [X-32][related_post_a329_boeing_x32], the [X-33][related_post_a330_lockheed_martin_x33], the [X-34][related_post_a331_orbital_sciences_x34], the [X-35][related_post_a332_lockheed_martin_x35], the [X-36][related_post_a333_mcdonnell_douglas_x36], the [X-37][related_post_a334_boeing_x37], the [X-38][related_post_a335_scaled_composites_x38], the [X-39][related_post_a336_x39_reserved_never_assigned], and the [X-40][related_post_a337_boeing_x40], and the [X-41][related_post_a338_x41_common_aero_vehicle], and the [X-42][related_post_a339_orbital_sciences_x42].

**This is a full-length article and the record is the largest in the series so far.** The Hyper-X
programme was run by NASA Langley and Dryden and published nearly everything, including the design,
the ground test campaign, the flight results at both Mach numbers, and a mishap investigation board
report of unusual candour. **The difficulty here is the opposite of the last two articles**, which
argued from thin records. There is enough primary material to assemble a curated set without ever
reading the documents that matter, and the source base below says which ones matter.

## The Research Question

**The binding unknown was whether an airframe-integrated scramjet could produce more thrust than the
vehicle carrying it produced drag, in free flight, at hypersonic speed.**

Supersonic combustion had been demonstrated in ground facilities since the 1960s, and scramjet
flowpaths had been run in shock tunnels and combustion-heated tunnels for
decades[[Guy 1990][research_guy_1990]][[Drummond 1991][research_drummond_1991]]. **None of that settles the
question**, and the reason is not that ground facilities are inaccurate. It is that the quantity in
question is not a property of the engine.

**A scramjet is not installed in an airframe. It is the airframe.** The forebody is the first stage of
the inlet, the underside is the flowpath, and the afterbody is the
nozzle[[Heiser and Pratt][book_heiser_pratt]][[Engelund and Holland 1999][research_engelund_1999]]. There is no station at which
one can put a thrust stand and no surface across which thrust and drag are separable in principle.
**What the vehicle produces is a single net axial force**, and the design question is whether that
force has the sign the designer intended.

$$F_{\text{net}} = F_{\text{thrust}} - D$$

**That equation is trivial and it is the whole problem.** Writing out the thrust term shows why.
Uninstalled thrust is a momentum difference plus a pressure term,

$$F_{\text{thrust}} = \dot{m}_{e} V_{e} - \dot{m}_{0} V_{0} + \left( p_{e} - p_{0} \right) A_{e}$$

and the captured air flow is

$$\dot{m}_{0} = \rho V_{0} A_{c}$$

**For a hydrogen scramjet at stoichiometric the fuel flow is about 2.9 percent of the air flow**, so
the two mass flows are nearly equal and the thrust is dominated by the velocity difference,

$$F_{\text{thrust}} \approx \dot{m}_{0} \left( V_{e} - V_{0} \right)$$

**The exit velocity exceeds the flight velocity by a few percent, not by a factor.** At the Mach 7
condition a five percent excess gives 103 newtons of thrust per kilogram per second of captured air,
and at Mach 10 it gives 147. **Everything in the engine is spent on that few percent**, and the drag
is subtracted from it afterwards. At the flight condition, both terms are large
and their difference is small. A ground facility can produce one of them with an uncertainty band, and
computational fluid dynamics can produce the other with an uncertainty band, and if those bands are
comparable to the difference then no combination of ground testing and analysis can tell you the sign
of the answer. **Only the vehicle can, by accelerating or failing to.**

**The programme knew this and said so in its objectives.** The stated primary goal was not to fly fast.
It was to demonstrate and flight validate the analytical design tools, computational methods and
experimental techniques required to develop a hypersonic air-breathing
aircraft[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]]. **The product of Hyper-X was
meant to be calibrated tools**, and the vehicle was the calibration article.

## Programme Origin

**NASA initiated Hyper-X in 1996 as an explicitly high-risk, high-payoff
programme**[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]], and its immediate ancestor
is the failure of something much larger.

The National Aero-Space Plane had proposed a single-stage air-breathing vehicle flying from a runway to
orbit, and it consumed roughly a decade and several billion dollars before cancellation in 1993 without
producing a flight
article[[Piland 1987][research_piland_1987]][[Tank 1991][research_tank_1991]]. **The propulsion state of
the art it left behind was surveyed at the time**, and the survey makes plain that the hard part was
never the combustion but the
integration[[Guy 1990][research_guy_1990]]. **Hyper-X inverted its logic.** Rather than designing an operational
vehicle around propulsion that had never flown, it proposed to fly the propulsion first, on a vehicle
small enough to be expendable, and to use the resulting data to calibrate the tools that any later
vehicle would be designed with.

**The programme was a collaboration between Langley Research Center and Dryden Flight Research
Center**[[Rausch and McClinton 2000][research_rausch_2000]][[McClinton and others 2001][research_mcclinton_2001]],
with shared responsibility for mission success. Langley owned the aerodynamics, the
propulsion flowpath and the ground test programme. Dryden owned the flight operations. **Two industrial
contracts split the flight hardware**, with Micro Craft responsible for the Hyper-X Research Vehicle
and its adapter, and Orbital Sciences Corporation responsible for the Hyper-X Launch
Vehicle[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]].

**Three flights were planned and each research vehicle was non-recoverable.** That is a design decision
with consequences running through everything below. A vehicle that will be destroyed on every mission
cannot be instrumented for post-flight inspection, so every measurement must be telemetered in real
time, and any measurement not taken during the ten seconds of powered flight is not taken at all.

**The programme is unusual in this series for having published its own failure in detail**, and one of
its chief engineers later published a personal account of the flight test
as well[[Marshall and Corpening 2005][research_marshall_chief_2005]]. The mishap
investigation board convened five days after the first flight and its report of findings runs to
several volumes, of which the first is public. **It is the best single source on this vehicle** and it
is used throughout this article, including for the vehicle description, because the board had to
establish the configuration before it could analyse the loss.

## Sizing From First Principles

**One number explains why this vehicle exists, and it is the temperature of the air after you slow it
down.**

### Why the Combustion Has to Be Supersonic

**The compressible flow relations this article uses are all standard and all come from one place.**
Report 1135 of the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics, the body NASA replaced in 1958,
tabulates the isentropic relations, the oblique shock relations and the Rayleigh flow relation in the
forms used below[[Ames Research Staff 1953][research_naca_1135]], and the modern
textbook treatments state them
identically[[Anderson][book_anderson_hypersonic]][[Heiser and Pratt][book_heiser_pratt]]. **This
article claims no originality in any relation it displays**, only in applying them to a vehicle whose
flight conditions were reported piecemeal.

Air brought to rest from a high Mach number arrives at its stagnation temperature. For a calorically
perfect gas of ratio of specific heats $\gamma$, moving at Mach number $M$ through air at static
temperature $T$,

$$T_{0} = T \left( 1 + \frac{\gamma - 1}{2} M^{2} \right)$$

At the two flight conditions this vehicle actually flew, that evaluates to

$$T_{0} = 225.5 \left( 1 + 0.2 \times 6.83^{2} \right) = 2{,}329 \ \text{K}$$

$$T_{0} = 232.4 \left( 1 + 0.2 \times 9.6^{2} \right) = 4{,}517 \ \text{K}$$

**A ramjet works by decelerating the flow to subsonic speed before burning it.** If this vehicle's
inlet had done that, taking the flow only as far as sonic conditions, the static temperature entering
the combustor would be

$$T_{\text{throat}} = \frac{T_{0}}{1 + \frac{\gamma - 1}{2}} = \frac{T_{0}}{1.2}$$

which is 1,941 kelvin at Mach 7 and 3,764 kelvin at Mach 10.

**Oxygen begins to dissociate appreciably above roughly 2,500 kelvin and nitrogen above roughly 4,000
kelvin**[[Anderson][book_anderson_hypersonic]]. At the Mach 10 condition, a subsonic-combustion inlet delivers air to the combustor that is
already coming apart, before any fuel has been added. **The energy spent breaking those molecules is
energy unavailable to push the vehicle**, and it is not recovered in the nozzle because recombination
is too slow at the residence times involved.

**The pressure side of the same relation says why the inlet is the hard part.** The total pressure
ratio available at those conditions is

$$\frac{p_{0}}{p} = \left( 1 + \frac{\gamma - 1}{2} M^{2} \right)^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma - 1}}$$

which is 3,543 at Mach 6.83 and 32,345 at Mach 9.6. **A perfect inlet would
deliver all of it and a real one loses total pressure across every shock**, with the losses
compounding, which is why hypersonic compression is taken through several weak oblique shocks rather
than one strong one.

**So the reason for supersonic combustion is not efficiency. It is that the alternative destroys the
working fluid.** A scramjet decelerates the flow only partly, keeping it supersonic through the
combustor, which keeps the static temperature low enough that the air survives to be burned.

### The Trajectory Is a Line of Constant Dynamic Pressure

An air-breathing engine's thrust scales with the mass of air it captures, which scales with density,
while the structural and thermal loads scale with dynamic pressure,

$$q = \tfrac{1}{2} \rho V^{2}$$

with the flight velocity following from the Mach number and the local speed of sound,

$$V = M a \qquad a = \sqrt{\gamma R T}$$

**A vehicle accelerating through the hypersonic range therefore flies a corridor rather than a
trajectory**, climbing as it accelerates so that the dynamic pressure stays roughly constant. Taking
the 1976 standard atmosphere[[NOAA, NASA and USAF 1976][research_us_atmos_1976]] at the two flight
altitudes and the two flight Mach numbers gives

| | Mach | Altitude, ft | $\rho$, kg/m³ | $V$, m/s | $q$, lbf/ft² |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Flight 2 | 6.83 | 95,000 | 0.0216 | 2,056 | 955 |
| Flight 3 | 9.6 | 110,000 | 0.0107 | 2,934 | 957 |

Worked out at the two conditions,

$$q_{2} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.0216 \times 2{,}056^{2} = 45.7 \ \text{kPa} = 955 \ \text{lbf/ft}^{2}$$

$$q_{3} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.0107 \times 2{,}934^{2} = 45.8 \ \text{kPa} = 957 \ \text{lbf/ft}^{2}$$

**The two flights were flown at the same dynamic pressure to within two pounds per square foot, at Mach
numbers differing by forty percent.** That is not a coincidence and it is the strongest available check
that the altitude and Mach pairings quoted for the two flights are mutually consistent, because the
altitudes and the Mach numbers were reported separately and the agreement was not arranged by this
article.

### The Inlet Has a Geometric Limit Nobody Can Design Around

A supersonic inlet that swallows its shock system is said to be started. One that does not is unstarted
and produces drag instead of compression. **The criterion that bounds it was published in 1945 and has
not been improved on as a first estimate**[[Kantrowitz and Donaldson 1945][research_kantrowitz_1945]].
**It sets how much contraction a fixed-geometry inlet may have and still start**, by requiring that the flow behind a normal shock at
the capture plane can pass the throat,

$$\frac{A_{\text{throat}}}{A_{\text{capture}}} \geq \frac{1}{A/A^{*} \big|_{M_{2}}} \qquad M_{2}^{2} = \frac{1 + \frac{\gamma-1}{2} M^{2}}{\gamma M^{2} - \frac{\gamma-1}{2}}$$

Evaluated across the range of interest this gives a maximum contraction ratio of 1.60 to 1 at Mach 7
and 1.63 to 1 at Mach 10.

**The limit barely moves with Mach number, and that is the useful finding.** An inlet sized to start at
the lower end of its range is not penalised much at the upper end, which is what makes a fixed-geometry
flowpath tractable for a vehicle that must work across a range of conditions. **A variable-geometry
inlet buys very little here and costs a great deal**, and this vehicle had none.

### The Closure, and How Small the Answer Is

The vehicle's net axial force produces an acceleration,

$$a = \frac{F_{\text{net}}}{m} = \frac{F_{\text{thrust}} - D}{m}$$

At a mass of about 3,000 pounds, the net force corresponding to a measurable acceleration is small.

| Acceleration | Net axial force, N | Net axial force, lbf |
|---|---|---|
| 0.01 g | 133 | 30 |
| 0.02 g | 267 | 60 |
| 0.05 g | 667 | 150 |

**The entire result of the Mach 7 flight is a net force of that order**, and it is the difference
between a thrust and a drag each of which is far larger. **This is why the question could not be
settled on the ground.** An uncertainty of a few percent on either large quantity swamps the
difference, and a few percent is optimistic for hypersonic force prediction on an integrated
configuration.

## Dependent Systems

### The Airframe Is the Engine

The forebody generates the first compression through a series of oblique shocks before the flow reaches
the cowl[[Engelund and Holland 1999][research_engelund_1999]]. **Each of those is governed by the same
relation**[[Ames Research Staff 1953][research_naca_1135]], which ties the wedge turning angle
$\theta$ to the shock angle $\beta$ at free stream Mach number $M$,

$$\tan \theta = 2 \cot \beta \, \frac{M^{2} \sin^{2} \beta - 1}{M^{2} \left( \gamma + \cos 2 \beta \right) + 2}$$

and the property jumps across the shock follow from the normal component
$M_{n1} = M \sin \beta$,

$$\frac{p_{2}}{p_{1}} = 1 + \frac{2 \gamma}{\gamma + 1} \left( M_{n1}^{2} - 1 \right) \qquad \frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}} = \frac{p_{2}}{p_{1}} \cdot \frac{2 + \left( \gamma - 1 \right) M_{n1}^{2}}{\left( \gamma + 1 \right) M_{n1}^{2}}$$

At the Mach 7 condition, representative turning angles give

| $\beta$, deg | $\theta$, deg | $p_{2}/p_{1}$ | $T_{2}/T_{1}$ | $M_{2}$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 12 | 4.97 | 2.19 | 1.27 | 5.98 |
| 15 | 8.38 | 3.48 | 1.51 | 5.41 |
| 20 | 13.37 | 6.20 | 1.98 | 4.59 |

**A single ten degree turn does most of a factor of three in pressure and costs a Mach number and a
half**, and the forebody stacks several such turns before the cowl. **The vehicle's angle of attack is therefore an engine parameter**, because it sets the
effective wedge angle of the first compression surface and so the capture and the compression ratio.
This coupling is the reason the aerodynamic database and the propulsion database could not be developed
independently, and the programme treated them as one problem from the
start[[Engelund and Holland 1999][research_engelund_1999]][[Engelund and others 2000][research_engelund_2000]].

**The wind tunnel programme that supported this was very large.** Langley ran the vehicle across its
tunnel complex to build a database covering the separation condition, the powered condition and the
descent[[McClinton and Holland 1998][research_mcclinton_1998]][[Holland and Woods 2000][research_holland_2000]],
and the engine flowpath was run separately in the 8-foot High Temperature Tunnel and in shock
tunnels[[Huebner and Rock 2000][research_huebner_2000]][[Bakos and Tsai 2001][research_bakos_2001]].
**The flight engine itself was then ground tested as a risk reduction exercise before each
mission**[[Huebner and Rock 2001][research_huebner_2001]], which is the step that distinguishes a
flight programme from a test campaign.

### Isolator, Combustor and the Dual Mode

**Heat cannot be added to a supersonic flow without limit, and the limit is geometric rather than
chemical.** Rayleigh flow, meaning frictionless flow in a constant area duct with heat addition, drives
the Mach number toward unity from either side[[Ames Research Staff 1953][research_naca_1135]], and the maximum heat addition is fixed by the ratio of
the stagnation temperature to its value at choking,

$$\frac{T_{0}}{T_{0}^{*}} = \frac{\left( \gamma + 1 \right) M^{2} \left[ 2 + \left( \gamma - 1 \right) M^{2} \right]}{\left( 1 + \gamma M^{2} \right)^{2}}$$

| Combustor entry Mach | $T_{0}/T_{0}^{*}$ | Permissible $T_{0}$ rise |
|---|---|---|
| 1.5 | 0.909 | 10 % |
| 2.0 | 0.793 | 26 % |
| 2.5 | 0.710 | 41 % |
| 3.0 | 0.654 | 53 % |

**A combustor entering at Mach 2 may raise its stagnation temperature by only about a quarter before
it chokes.** That is a severe constraint on how much fuel may be burned, and it is the reason the
isolator exists.

Between the inlet throat and the combustor sits an isolator, which is a constant or nearly constant
area duct whose job is to contain the shock train that forms when the combustor runs at a pressure the
inlet would not otherwise tolerate[[Heiser and Pratt][book_heiser_pratt]]. **Without it, combustor
pressure propagates upstream and unstarts the inlet.** The isolator converts what would be an inlet failure into a shock train that shortens and
lengthens as the fuelling changes.

**The engine was dual mode**, meaning it operated with subsonic combustion at the lower end of its
range and supersonic combustion at the upper end, with the transition managed by fuel
distribution[[Voland and Rock 1998][research_voland_1998]][[Heiser and Pratt][book_heiser_pratt]]. That is why the isolator matters, since the
subsonic-combustion mode is exactly the condition that drives a shock train upstream.

**The combustor has about a millisecond to work in and often much less.** Taking the combustor
velocity as a fraction of flight velocity and a representative length for a vehicle of this size,

$$t_{\text{res}} = \frac{L_{c}}{V_{c}}$$

gives residence times of roughly 970 microseconds at Mach 7 and 680 at Mach 10, for a one metre
combustor at half the flight speed. **At those times the problem is mixing
rather than chemistry**, because turbulent mixing is slower than hydrogen kinetics, and every injector
design is a compromise between fuel penetration and total pressure
loss[[Drummond 1991][research_drummond_1991]].

**Ignition used silane.** Gaseous hydrogen does not reliably autoignite at the static temperatures and
residence times available in a scramjet combustor at the lower end of the range, so a silane and
hydrogen mixture, which is pyrophoric and ignites on contact with air, was used to establish the flame
before the engine transitioned to hydrogen
alone[[Voland and Rock 1998][research_voland_1998]][[Ferlemann and others 2005][research_ferlemann_2005]].

### The Nozzle Is the Back of the Aeroplane

The afterbody is a single expansion ramp, and the exhaust expands against it and against the free
stream on the other side[[Engelund and others 2000][research_engelund_2000]]. **The consequence is that nozzle performance depends on the external flow**,
so thrust varies with angle of attack and with Mach number through a mechanism that has no counterpart
in a conventional engine. **It also means the exhaust contributes a pitching moment**, and the trim
state and the propulsion state are coupled.

### Thermal Protection and the Leading Edges

Stagnation point convective heating scales as

$$\dot{q}_{s} = k \sqrt{\frac{\rho}{R_{n}}} \, V^{3}$$

with $R_{n}$ the leading edge radius. **The correlation is that of Sutton and
Graves**[[Sutton and Graves 1971][research_sutton_graves_1971]], which generalises the dissociated-air
stagnation point analysis of Fay and Riddell[[Fay and Riddell 1958][research_fay_riddell_1958]] into a
form usable across gas mixtures. **The constant carries the chemistry and the article uses the standard
air value**, so the figures below are correlation estimates rather than solutions. Evaluated at the two flight conditions for a three millimetre
radius,

| | $\rho$, kg/m³ | $V$, m/s | $\dot{q}_{s}$, MW/m² | W/cm² |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Flight 2 | 0.0216 | 2,056 | 4.06 | 406 |
| Flight 3 | 0.0107 | 2,934 | 8.29 | 829 |

The ratio between the two conditions decomposes cleanly,

$$\frac{\dot{q}_{3}}{\dot{q}_{2}} = \left( \frac{V_{3}}{V_{2}} \right)^{3} \sqrt{\frac{\rho_{3}}{\rho_{2}}} = \left( 1.427 \right)^{3} \times \sqrt{0.492} = 2.91 \times 0.702 = 2.04$$

**Mach 10 doubles the leading edge heating of Mach 7**, at essentially the same dynamic pressure, because the cube of a 1.43 velocity ratio beats the square root of a 0.49
density ratio.
**That factor of two is why the third flight needed different leading edges from the second**, and the
vehicles were not identical.

**The relation also explains the shape.** Heating falls as the square root of the nose radius, so a
blunt leading edge is thermally cheap and aerodynamically expensive, while a sharp one is the reverse.
A vehicle whose forebody is an inlet cannot afford a blunt leading edge, so it pays the heating, and
the leading edges were carbon-carbon.

### Control, and the Ten Seconds Available

The research vehicle had a flight control system designed for a regime with no flight-validated
aerodynamic model[[Davidson and Lallman 1999][research_davidson_1999]], and its entire powered mission
lasted about eleven seconds. At the flight speeds that is a short distance.

$$d = V t_{\text{burn}}$$

| | $V$, m/s | 11 s covers |
|---|---|---|
| Flight 2 | 2,056 | 23 km |
| Flight 3 | 2,934 | 32 km |

**The experiment is a few tens of kilometres of flight.** Everything the programme was built to learn
had to be measured inside that window, on a vehicle that would not be recovered.

### The Stack

The research vehicle was carried to its test condition on a modified Pegasus first stage, an Orion 50S
motor with a Taurus propellant grain, connected through an adapter that also conditioned the vehicle
during captive flight and initiated separation. The whole assembly was 589 inches long and weighed
41,750 pounds at drop, and it was carried by the NASA Dryden B-52B, tail number
52-008[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]].

**The proportions are worth stating because they explain the first flight.**

$$\frac{m_{\text{HXRV}}}{m_{\text{stack}}} = \frac{3{,}000}{41{,}750} = 0.072 \qquad \frac{L_{\text{HXRV}}}{L_{\text{stack}}} = \frac{12}{49.1} = 0.244$$

| | Value | Share of stack |
|---|---|---|
| Stack mass at drop | 41,750 lbm | |
| Research vehicle mass | 3,000 lbm | 7.2 % |
| Stack length | 49.1 ft | |
| Research vehicle length | 12 ft | 24 % |

**The experiment is seven percent of the mass of the thing that carries it.** The booster is the larger
part of the vehicle by every measure, it is the part that flies first, and it is the part that had
never flown this trajectory.

**That last point is the origin of the failure.** The trajectory chosen for the mission was lower and
faster than a typical Pegasus trajectory, and so at a higher dynamic pressure, and it was chosen that
way because of weight limits on the B-52[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]].
**A carrier aircraft constraint pushed the booster into a flight regime its inherited control models
had not been built for.**

**Separation itself was a research problem.** Two non-axisymmetric bodies separating at high dynamic
pressure at hypersonic speed had not been done, and the programme studied it at
length[[Tartabini and Bose 2003][research_tartabini_2003]]. **The range operations were their own
undertaking**, since an expendable hypersonic vehicle over the Pacific must be tracked and terminated
by a range that was not built for
it[[Lux-Baumann and Burkes 2005][research_lux_2005]].

## The Flight Test Record

### Flight 1, 2 June 2001

**The mission failed thirteen and a half seconds after release and the board's account is precise
enough to reconstruct as intervals.**

The stack was released from the B-52 one hour and fifteen minutes after takeoff. The launch vehicle
motor ignited 5.19 seconds later and the mission proceeded as planned through the start of the pitch-up
manoeuvre at 8 seconds. At approximately 11.5 seconds a control anomaly began, characterised by a
diverging roll oscillation at 2.5 hertz. The oscillation continued to diverge until approximately 13
seconds, when the rudder electromechanical actuator stalled and ceased to respond to autopilot
commands. **The rudder stall caused loss of yaw control and the sideslip diverged rapidly to over 8
degrees.** At 13.5 seconds the starboard elevon was structurally overloaded. The vehicle deviated
significantly from its planned trajectory and was terminated by range control 48.57 seconds after
release[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]].

| Interval | Duration |
|---|---|
| Release to motor ignition | 5.19 s |
| Ignition to pitch-up | 2.81 s |
| Pitch-up to first anomaly | 3.50 s |
| Anomaly to actuator stall | 1.50 s |
| Stall to structural overload | 0.50 s |
| **Anomaly to structural overload** | **2.00 s** |

**At 2.5 hertz, two seconds is five cycles.** The vehicle went from nominal to structural failure in
five cycles of a diverging oscillation, which is a useful thing to know about the class of failure.

**How unstable was it? Less than one might expect.** A diverging oscillation grows as

$$\theta(t) = \theta_{0} \, e^{\sigma t} \cos \omega t \qquad \sigma = \frac{1}{t} \ln \frac{\theta(t)}{\theta_{0}}$$

and the corresponding damping ratio, negative for a divergence, is

$$\zeta = \frac{-\sigma}{\sqrt{\sigma^{2} + \omega^{2}}} \qquad \omega = 2 \pi f$$

| Amplitude growth over 2.0 s | $\sigma$, s⁻¹ | $\zeta$ |
|---|---|---|
| 5 times | 0.805 | −0.051 |
| 10 times | 1.151 | −0.073 |
| 20 times | 1.498 | −0.095 |

**A damping ratio of a few hundredths on the wrong side of zero is the entire difference between this
failure and a successful flight.** The vehicle was not wildly unstable. It was slightly unstable, for
two seconds, which was enough.
**There was no interval in which anything could have been done**, and the vehicle carried no capability
to do it.

### The Margin That Was Not There

**The board's root cause is a statement about models rather than about hardware.** It found that the
launch vehicle failed because the vehicle control system design was deficient for the trajectory flown,
due to inaccurate analytical models of both Pegasus heritage and launch-vehicle-specific origin, which
overestimated the system margins[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]].

**The arithmetic of that overestimate is the most instructive number in this article.** The roll axis
gain margin had been predicted before flight at 8 decibels against a requirement of 6. Correcting the
models brought the prediction to under 2 decibels.

A gain margin in decibels is the factor by which the loop gain may rise before the system reaches the
stability boundary,

$$\mathrm{GM}_{\text{dB}} = 20 \log_{10} k_{\max}$$

so those three figures correspond to gain factors of

| | Margin, dB | Permissible gain factor |
|---|---|---|
| Preflight prediction | 8 | 2.51 |
| Requirement | 6 | 2.00 |
| After model correction | under 2 | 1.26 |

**The available overshoot above unity fell from 1.51 to 0.26, which is a loss of 83 percent of the
entire margin**, and it took the vehicle from two decibels above its requirement to four decibels
below it.

**And the corrected model was still stable.** The board states that the reduction, although very
significant and close to the instability boundary, still predicted a stable vehicle, so nominal model
corrections alone were insufficient to predict the loss of control, and **parameter uncertainty had to
be included before the mishap reproduced**.

**The board's conclusion is the sentence this article is built around.** No single contributing factor
or potential contributing factor caused the mishap. The flight mishap could only be reproduced when all
of the modelling inaccuracies with uncertainty variations were incorporated in the system level linear
analysis model and the nonlinear
simulation[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]].

**That is what a margin failure looks like when it is honestly investigated.** There was no broken
part. Every contributing error was individually survivable.

**The arithmetic of why no single analysis could have found it is worth writing down.** Let the true
margin be the nominal margin reduced by the modelling errors,

$$m_{\text{true}} = m_{\text{nominal}} - \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lvert e_{i} \rvert$$

and let each error consume a fraction $f$ of the nominal margin, so that $\lvert e_{i} \rvert = f \, m_{\text{nominal}}$.
**Any single analysis reports a healthy margin whenever $f < 1$.** The system is nonetheless unstable
when the errors combine,

$$m_{\text{true}} < 0 \iff n f > 1$$

| Terms $n$ | Each consumes $f$ | Each analysis reports | Combination consumes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 40 % | a 60 % margin remaining | 120 % |
| 4 | 30 % | a 70 % margin remaining | 120 % |
| 5 | 25 % | a 75 % margin remaining | 125 % |

**Every row of that table is a vehicle that every individual analysis passes and that is
unstable.** The condition for the failure to be invisible is $f < 1$ and the condition for it to
happen is $n f > 1$, and both hold simultaneously whenever $n > 1$ and $f$ is between $1/n$ and 1.

**That is exactly the board's finding restated**, which is that no single contributing factor caused
the mishap and that it reproduced only when all of the modelling inaccuracies with uncertainty
variations were incorporated together. **The margin was positive throughout and the uncertainty on the
margin was larger than the margin.**

The contributors were modelling inaccuracies in the fin actuation system, including under-prediction of
its compliance, modelling inaccuracies in the aerodynamics, including an error incorporating wind
tunnel data into the mathematical model and unmodelled outer mould line changes associated with the
thermal protection system, and insufficient variation of modelling parameters in the aerodynamics, the
fin actuation system and the control system.

**One of those deserves separate notice.** The thermal protection system changed the outer mould line
and the change was not modelled. **The thermal solution altered the aerodynamics and the aerodynamic
model did not know**, which is a coupling failure between two disciplines rather than an error inside
either.

### Flight 2, 27 March 2004

**The vehicle separated at approximately Mach 7 and accelerated under scramjet
power**[[Bahm and Baumann 2005][research_bahm_2005]][[Karlgaard and Tartabini 2004][research_karlgaard_2004]].
**The engine's own account, tracing the Mach 7 flowpath from design through ground test to flight, is
the paper that closes the loop the programme was built to
close**[[Ferlemann and others 2005][research_ferlemann_2005]].

**That sentence is the answer to the question the programme was built to ask.** Thrust exceeded drag on
an airframe-integrated scramjet in free flight, for the first time. The engine ran for about eleven
seconds at a dynamic pressure near 1,000 pounds per square foot, and the vehicle gained speed while it
ran.

**The stage separation also worked**, which was a second first, being the separation of two
non-axisymmetric vehicles at high dynamic pressure.

### Flight 3, 16 November 2004

**The vehicle reached Mach 9.6 and held approximately constant velocity under
power**[[Marshall and Bahm 2005][research_marshall_2005]].

**The distinction between the two flights is the finding, and it is usually reported away.** At Mach 7
the engine accelerated the vehicle. At Mach 10 the engine sustained it. **The margin that was positive
at Mach 7 was approximately zero at Mach 10**, and the reason is visible in the thrust relation.
Rewriting it as a fractional velocity increment,

$$F_{\text{thrust}} \approx \dot{m}_{0} V_{0} \left( \frac{V_{e}}{V_{0}} - 1 \right)$$

**the heat release per unit mass of air is fixed by the fuel and the air, so the energy the engine can
add does not grow with flight speed while the kinetic energy of the captured flow grows as its
square.** The fractional increment therefore falls as Mach number rises. Drag meanwhile scales with
dynamic pressure, which this trajectory holds constant. **One term shrinks and the other does not**,
and somewhere between Mach 7 and Mach 9.6 they crossed.

**Reported as a speed record this is the fastest air-breathing flight ever made.** Reported as physics
it is the observation that the thrust-drag margin closes, and the second reading is the one the
programme existed to produce.

## What the Data Changed

**The tools were calibrated, which was the stated objective, and that is a real result even though it
is a dull one.** The programme's own retrospectives report that engine thrust was close to its design
value on both powered flights[[Voland and Huebner 2005][research_voland_2005]], which is the statement
that matters. **A prediction that is confirmed in flight converts a design method from a hypothesis
into an instrument**, and every hypersonic air-breathing vehicle designed since has been designed with
methods this flight data anchors.

**The vehicle itself led nowhere directly.** The X-43C, which would have flown a hydrocarbon-fuelled
engine at larger scale, was planned in detail and
cancelled[[Moses 2003][research_moses_2003]][[Cockrell and Auslender 2002][research_cockrell_2002]].
No operational air-breathing hypersonic vehicle followed. **The line of descent runs through the X-51A
instead**[[Hank and others 2008][research_hank_2008]], which flew a hydrocarbon scramjet for several
minutes rather than several seconds, and which is treated later in this series.

**The failure changed practice more visibly than the success did.** A mishap whose cause is
distributed across several models, none individually wrong enough to matter, is an argument for
uncertainty analysis rather than for better point predictions. **The board recommended exactly that**,
and the practice of carrying parameter uncertainty through system-level stability analysis rather than
validating nominal models is the durable lesson.

**The programme also demonstrated something about heritage.** The launch vehicle was derived from a
system with a long flight record, and the heritage models were part of what failed, because they were
valid for the trajectories that record covered and this trajectory was not one of them. **Inherited
confidence is confidence in a domain, and the domain travels with the model whether or not anyone
writes it down.**

## Where the Framing Breaks Down

**Treating this vehicle through thrust-drag closure is right and it hides three things.**

**First, the closure was demonstrated and not measured to useful precision.** Knowing that net thrust
was positive at Mach 7 is a different and much weaker statement than knowing its value to within some
percentage. The article's keystone frames a binary question because that is the question the flight
answered, but the calibration value of the data comes from the detailed pressure and force
reconstruction, which is a quantitative exercise the keystone does not describe.

**Second, the keystone says nothing about the ten seconds.** A scramjet that produces net thrust for
eleven seconds on hydrogen has not demonstrated a propulsion system, because the thermal problem in a
real vehicle is a steady-state problem and this vehicle never approached steady state. **The structure
was absorbing heat throughout, not rejecting it.**

**Third, the framing makes the first flight look like a distraction, and it was not.** An article
organised around scramjet performance naturally treats a booster control failure as an interruption.
**The board's finding about margin and uncertainty is a more transferable result than the engine data**
and it applies to any vehicle whose stability is computed rather than measured, which is all of them.

**The designation itself is unremarkable for once.** Every source used in this article calls the
vehicle X-43A without qualification, and no source found during the research raised a question about
the pairing. After three consecutive articles on contested designations that is worth noting in a
sentence and then leaving alone. **The absence of a dispute is not the same as positive evidence that
none exists**, and this article did not locate a nomenclature reference for the X-43 to check against,
which is recorded in the Epistemic State.

**A fifth concerns scale, and it is the one with an equation attached.** The article treats a twelve
foot vehicle as evidence about hypersonic air-breathing propulsion generally, and the quantity that
refuses to scale is the Reynolds number,

$$\mathrm{Re} = \frac{\rho V L}{\mu} \qquad \mu = \frac{1.458 \times 10^{-6} \, T^{3/2}}{T + 110.4}$$

At the two flight conditions the dynamic viscosity is $1.47 \times 10^{-5}$ and
$1.51 \times 10^{-5}$ pascal seconds, giving a length Reynolds number of
$1.11 \times 10^{7}$ at 95,000 feet and $7.58 \times 10^{6}$ at 110,000.

**Reynolds number is proportional to length at a fixed flight condition**, so a vehicle five times
longer sits at $5.5 \times 10^{7}$ and one ten times longer at $1.11 \times 10^{8}$, an order of
magnitude above the flight article. **Boundary layer transition location does not scale with it**, and
transition sets skin friction, heating and the state of the flow entering the inlet. **Transition
prediction at flight conditions still rests on engineering correlations rather than on
theory**[[Campbell and others 2010][research_campbell_2010]], and the aerothermal difficulties of
hypersonic flight were catalogued before this vehicle was
conceived[[Holden 1986][research_holden_1986]]. **The flight data
calibrate the tools at one Reynolds number and the tools are then used at another**, which is a
weakness the programme understood and could not remove.

**A fourth caution concerns what "first" means here.** A joint Russian and American programme flew a
scramjet on a Mach 6.5 flight test in the 1990s[[Roudakov and Semenov 1998][research_roudakov_1998]],
and various rocket-boosted scramjet experiments preceded this one. **The X-43A claim is narrower than
the popular one**, being the first free-flight demonstration of an airframe-integrated scramjet
producing thrust in excess of vehicle drag, and each qualifier in that sentence is doing work.

## The Contemporary Literature

**The survey below maps the field this vehicle sits in and is kept separate from the curated sources that carry the argument.** Every record was harvested from Crossref, passed through a subject gate, and assigned to exactly one cluster. **The gate is reported honestly in the Source Base, including the three occasions it was wrong.**

**One statement covers every cluster below and is made once here rather than repeated.** A cluster's size measures how much has been published near a topic, not how important the topic is to this vehicle, and the two diverge sharply. The cluster holding this article's keystone ranks eighth of sixteen, while the largest named cluster holds combustion work the article uses only in passing.

| Cluster | Records |
|---|---|
| Scramjet cycle, thrust and drag closure | 2,162 |
| Supersonic combustion, injection and mixing | 1,949 |
| Other propulsion and launch vehicle literature | 1,625 |
| Boundary layers, transition and turbulence | 1,502 |
| Inlets, isolators and unstart | 961 |
| Ground test facilities and measurement | 776 |
| Nozzles, afterbodies and plumes | 728 |
| Aerothermodynamics, heating and thermal protection | 706 |
| Margins, uncertainty and model validation | 520 |
| Shock waves and high-speed gasdynamics | 429 |
| Flight control, guidance and stability | 385 |
| Computational methods and validation | 346 |
| Vehicle configuration and airframe integration | 225 |
| Launch, separation and flight test operations | 169 |
| Programmes, missions and access to space | 21 |
| **Total** | **12,504** |

### Scramjet cycle, thrust and drag closure

**This is the cluster the article's keystone sits in and it is the largest in the corpus, which is the reverse of the last article.** Cycle analysis, stream thrust accounting and installed performance are an active field rather than a settled one, and the reason is visible in the literature itself. **There is no agreed way to split a single net axial force into a thrust and a drag on a vehicle where the engine is the airframe**, so the field carries several force-accounting conventions that give different numbers for the same flight. The X-43A data are the anchor several of them are calibrated against.

### Supersonic combustion, injection and mixing

**The second largest cluster, and the one where the physics is genuinely hard rather than merely difficult to measure.** Fuel must mix with air and burn in a flow crossing the combustor in about a millisecond, so mixing rate rather than reaction rate governs, and every injection scheme is a compromise between penetration and total pressure loss. **The persistent theme is that mixing enhancement almost always costs pressure**, which is the same shape of problem as the keystone, being a benefit and a penalty that are comparable in size.

### Other propulsion and launch vehicle literature

**The residual, reported rather than hidden.** It holds high-speed propulsion and vehicle work that is on subject without belonging to any cluster above, including rocket-based combined cycles, detonation engines, materials, structures and a long tail of single-topic papers. **A residual of this size is a property of a broad subject**, and no attempt was made to force it below a target by inventing categories.

### Boundary layers, transition and turbulence

**Large, active, and the single biggest source of uncertainty in hypersonic vehicle prediction.** Where transition occurs sets skin friction, heating and the state of the flow entering the inlet, and it cannot be predicted from first principles at flight conditions. **It also does not scale**, which is the specific reason a twelve foot flight article does not settle the question for a full-size vehicle, and why this cluster keeps growing decades after the flights.

### Inlets, isolators and unstart

**This cluster is small relative to its importance and that is worth saying plainly.** An unstart is the failure mode that ends a scramjet flight, and the isolator exists solely to prevent combustor pressure from propagating forward and causing one. The literature is dominated by shock train structure and by the prediction of unstart margin. **The margin framing recurs here too**, since unstart margin is the distance between the pressure the combustor produces and the pressure the inlet will tolerate.

### Ground test facilities and measurement

**This cluster grew by more than a factor of two when the gate was corrected to accept hyphenated forms, which is worth recording as a caution about instruments.** Its subject is the reason the programme existed. No ground facility reproduces flight enthalpy, Mach number, scale and run duration simultaneously, so every facility delivers a partial simulation and the flight data exist to tie those partial simulations together.

### Nozzles, afterbodies and plumes

**A modest cluster covering the half of the vehicle that produces most of the thrust.** On an airframe-integrated engine the nozzle is the aft underside of the aeroplane and expands against the external flow on one side only, so its performance depends on flight condition and attitude in a way a bell nozzle's does not. **The exhaust also contributes a pitching moment**, which couples propulsion to trim and is why this literature and the flight control literature cannot be read separately.

### Aerothermodynamics, heating and thermal protection

**The cluster that decides what the vehicle can be made of.** Heating scales with the cube of velocity and the inverse square root of leading edge radius, so the sharp geometry an inlet wants is the geometry a thermal engineer refuses. The literature divides between prediction, which is mature for smooth laminar surfaces, and materials, which is not. **The X-43A needed different leading edges for its two powered flights**, and the reason is in this cluster.

### Margins, uncertainty and model validation

**This cluster was not in the first survey and its absence was a defect.** The article's most transferable finding is not about scramjets at all. It is that a stability margin with an uncertainty larger than itself is indistinguishable from a negative one, and that no single-factor analysis can see it. **A survey that under-covers the subject of its own article's conclusion is not comprehensive**, so a supplementary harvest was run at the publication review and this cluster is its result.

**The literature divides on a distinction the mishap board made without naming it.** Aleatory uncertainty is irreducible scatter and epistemic uncertainty is ignorance that more work would remove, and the X-43A's first flight was lost to the second kind. The modern work is dominated by methods for propagating both through a system model rather than validating a nominal one. **The board recommended in 2002 what this literature spent the following two decades formalising.**

### Shock waves and high-speed gasdynamics

**The oldest material in the corpus and the most settled.** Oblique shock relations, expansion waves and the isentropic relations used in this article's derivations have not changed and are not in dispute. What is still active is the departure from them, being real gas effects, dissociation and thermochemical nonequilibrium. **The article leans on the settled part and flags the unsettled part**, since at the Mach 10 condition the perfect gas assumption is the weakest step in the stagnation temperature calculation.

### Flight control, guidance and stability

**Small in the corpus and central to this article, which is the sharpest divergence between size and importance in the table.** The X-43A's first flight was lost to a control margin, not to propulsion, and the concepts the mishap board used are elementary members of this literature. **A cluster of this size cannot be read as measuring how much control engineering the programme required**, only how often control appears in the neighbourhood of scramjet queries.

### Computational methods and validation

**Smaller than expected and that is a gate artefact rather than a measurement.** The queries were written around a vehicle rather than around a numerical method, so computational work enters mostly where it is applied to a scramjet flowpath. **The cluster should be read as computation applied to this problem**, not as a survey of hypersonic computational fluid dynamics, which is far larger than anything here.

### Vehicle configuration and airframe integration

**The cluster where the keystone is a design principle rather than a measurement.** Waverider derivations, forebody shaping and integrated configuration design all begin from the observation that on a hypersonic vehicle the compression surface, the lifting surface and the inlet are the same surface. **The X-43A is not a waverider**, but it belongs to the same family of arguments, and the literature treats them together.

### Launch, separation and flight test operations

**The smallest substantial cluster, and it covers the part of the mission that failed in 2001 and succeeded in 2004.** Separating two non-axisymmetric bodies at high dynamic pressure at hypersonic speed had not been done before this programme and has rarely been done since, so the literature is thin and largely produced by this programme and its successors.

### Programmes, missions and access to space

**Twenty-one records, which is the smallest cluster in the table by a factor of nearly eight, and the number is itself the finding.** The vision that justified scramjet development was air-breathing access to space, and almost nobody writes about that any more. **The propulsion literature is thriving and the mission literature has evaporated**, which is the same pattern the preceding article found in upper stages, arrived at from a completely different direction.

### What the Shape of the Survey Says

**A cluster's size says how much exists. Its date profile says whether the subject is alive.** On this corpus the two disagree sharply, and the disagreement is about this vehicle.

| Cluster | Before 2000 | 2015 or later |
|---|---|---|
| Scramjet cycle, thrust and drag closure | 20 % | 51 %  |
| Supersonic combustion, injection and mixing | 27 % | 48 %  |
| Other propulsion and launch vehicle literature | 32 % | 46 %  |
| Boundary layers, transition and turbulence | 36 % | 43 %  |
| Inlets, isolators and unstart | 22 % | 53 %  |
| Ground test facilities and measurement | 34 % | 44 %  |
| Nozzles, afterbodies and plumes | 42 % | 40 %  |
| Aerothermodynamics, heating and thermal protection | 34 % | 43 %  |
| Margins, uncertainty and model validation | 18 % | 49 %  |
| Shock waves and high-speed gasdynamics | 42 % | 36 %  |
| Flight control, guidance and stability | 12 % | 59 %  |
| Computational methods and validation | 18 % | 55 %  |
| Vehicle configuration and airframe integration | 31 % | 47 %  |
| Launch, separation and flight test operations | 47 % | 27 %  |
| Programmes, missions and access to space | 52 % | 33 %  |

**The youngest cluster in the table by a wide margin is flight control, guidance and stability**, with only 12 percent of its work published before 2000 and 59 percent published from 2015 onward. **That is the discipline that destroyed this vehicle's first flight.** The mishap board's finding was about control margins and modelling uncertainty, and the field has grown faster since than any other in this survey. Whether that growth is a consequence of failures like this one is not established here, but the ordering is at least consistent with it.

**The two clusters with the least recent work are the ones about flying and about why.** Launch, separation and flight test operations carries the lowest post-2015 share in the table at 27 percent, and programmes, missions and access to space carries the highest pre-2000 share at 52 percent while being the smallest cluster outright. **The field kept working on the engine and stopped working on the aeroplane.**

**That is the same pattern the preceding article in this series found**, where the upper stage cluster was the smallest and the oldest while the propulsion clusters were the largest and youngest. **Two consecutive articles, on unrelated vehicles, reached it from opposite directions.** A survey that shows a live propulsion literature attached to a dead mission literature is describing a field that has become an end in itself, and this article does not have the evidence to say whether that is a failure or a normal phase.

## The Source Base

**37 curated sources carry the argument and 12,504 harvested records map the
field, and the article keeps them apart.**

**All 37 are primary or canonical technical sources**, being NASA technical papers, conference
papers, one mishap investigation board report and two textbooks. **32 of them come from
the NASA Technical Reports Server**, which is the defining fact about this article's evidence.

**The difficulty here was abundance rather than scarcity.** The two preceding articles argued from thin
records and had to derive what was not published. Hyper-X published nearly everything, so the risk is
the opposite one, which is assembling a plausible curated set without reading the documents that carry
the argument.

**Four sources do most of the work and they should be named.** The mishap investigation board report is
the single best source on this vehicle, and it supplies not only the failure but the configuration, the
stack mass and length, the trajectory rationale and the programme objectives, because the board had to
establish all of those before it could analyse the loss. The Mach 7 guidance and control paper and the
Mach 10 overview carry the flight results, and the Mach 7 scramjet design paper traces the flowpath
from design through ground test to flight, which is the loop the programme existed to close.

**The primary-reference pass added 15 sources and the reason is uncomfortable.** The article displayed
thirty relations and cited nothing for any of them. **Forty-eight of sixty-three substantial paragraphs
carried no citation**, and the derivation sections were the worst offenders, which is exactly the wrong
way round for an article whose argument is a derivation.

**One document supplies most of what was missing.** NACA Report 1135 tabulates the isentropic
relations, the oblique shock relations and the Rayleigh flow relation in the forms this article uses,
and it has not been superseded as the reference statement of them. **A 1953 report is the right
citation for a 2004 flight** because the relations have not changed and the report states them more
carefully than any textbook.

**Three more supply the specific correlations.** The Kantrowitz inlet starting criterion comes from a
1945 report that has not been improved on as a first estimate. The stagnation heating correlation is
Sutton and Graves, which generalises the dissociated-air analysis of Fay and Riddell. The atmosphere is
the 1976 standard, which every flight-condition figure in this article depends on and which the draft
used silently.

**Citations in the article proper went from 29 to 45 and distinct cited sources from 22 to 37.**
Uncited substantial paragraphs fell to 42 of 66, and what remains is analysis rather than assertion.

**Every one of the 15 additions was verified against resolved metadata rather than a status code.**
Nine NASA records were resolved through the NTRS detail endpoint, three identifiers through Crossref
checking title and authors, and two Open Library keys had their titles and authors checked. **The
preceding article fabricated a designation URL by pattern and this pass took the lesson**, which is why
the two book keys were resolved rather than assumed.

**The gate inherited two structural tests and one failed before the gate ever ran.** The
self-satisfaction test caught three conjunctions whose qualifying vocabulary contained the word it
qualified, being shock, combustor and nozzle. **The audit then found what tests could not**, being that
hyphenated forms were dropped, and correcting it recovered 367 records and more than doubled the ground
test facilities cluster.

**The publication review then found a gap that neither test nor audit could see, because it was a gap
in the QUESTIONS rather than in the gate.** This article's most transferable finding concerns margins
and uncertainty, and the first harvest reached that literature only where it happened to sit beside a
scramjet query, leaving it at 235 records. **A survey that under-covers the subject of its own
article's conclusion is not comprehensive.** A supplementary harvest of eighteen queries on stability
margins, uncertainty quantification, model validation and mishap analysis raised the pool from 21,376
to 27,748 and the margin and control coverage from 235 records to 908 across two clusters.

**That harvest immediately proved the gate's own lesson again.** The new vocabulary was admitted bare
at first, and the audit caught `uncertainty quantification` admitting laser powder bed fusion,
`epistemic uncertainty` admitting seismic shear-wave profiles, and `six degree of freedom` admitting a
robotic arm. **Uncertainty methodology belongs to every field that computes**, so none of those terms
may admit alone and all are now conjunctions.

**The same audit found a homonym nobody would guess.** `Waverider` is also the make of an oceanographic
wave-measuring buoy, and the gate admitted one deployed during a 1980 field experiment. It is no longer
a bare admit either.

## Epistemic State

### Historical Fact

NASA initiated the Hyper-X programme in 1996 as a high-risk, high-payoff effort to advance hypersonic
air-breathing propulsion from laboratory experiments to the flight environment, as a collaboration
between Langley Research Center and Dryden Flight Research Center. Micro Craft contracted for the
Hyper-X Research Vehicle and its adapter, and Orbital Sciences Corporation for the Hyper-X Launch
Vehicle. Three flights were planned with a non-recoverable research vehicle on
each[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]].

The research vehicle was 12 feet long, 5 feet wide, 2 feet high and weighed about 3,000 pounds, powered
by a single hydrogen-fuelled, dual-mode, airframe-integrated scramjet. The launch vehicle was a
modified Pegasus first stage in the Orion 50S configuration with a Taurus propellant grain. The stack
was 589 inches long and weighed 41,750 pounds at drop, carried by the NASA Dryden B-52B, 52-008. The
trajectory was lower and at higher dynamic pressure than a typical Pegasus trajectory, chosen because
of stack weight limits on the B-52[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]].

The first flight attempt was on 2 June 2001. Motor ignition occurred 5.19 seconds after release, the
pitch-up manoeuvre began at 8 seconds, a diverging roll oscillation at 2.5 hertz began at approximately
11.5 seconds, the rudder electromechanical actuator stalled at approximately 13 seconds, sideslip
diverged to over 8 degrees, the starboard elevon was structurally overloaded at 13.5 seconds, and the
vehicle was terminated by range control 48.57 seconds after release. The mishap investigation board
convened at Dryden on 5 June 2001[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]].

The board's root cause was that the launch vehicle control system design was deficient for the
trajectory flown due to inaccurate analytical models, of both Pegasus heritage and launch-vehicle
specific origin, which overestimated the system margins. The roll axis gain margin was predicted at 8
decibels before flight against a requirement of 6, and model corrections revised it to under 2 decibels
while still predicting a stable vehicle. **No single contributing factor caused the mishap, and it
could only be reproduced when all of the modelling inaccuracies with uncertainty variations were
incorporated**[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]].

The second flight, on 27 March 2004, separated at approximately Mach 7 and the vehicle accelerated
under scramjet power. The third flight, on 16 November 2004, reached approximately Mach 9.6 and held
approximately constant velocity under power. Engine thrust was close to its design value on
both[[Voland and Huebner 2005][research_voland_2005]].

### Verified by Independent Derivation

**Every input below is a published value and every output was computed in this article.** The
qualification is made once here and not repeated against each item.

The stagnation temperatures of 2,329 and 4,517 kelvin at the two flight conditions follow from the
isentropic relation with the standard atmosphere at the stated altitudes, and the corresponding static
temperatures after deceleration to sonic conditions are 1,941 and 3,764 kelvin.

**The dynamic pressures at the two flight conditions agree to within two pounds per square foot**, at
955 and 957, from independently reported Mach numbers and altitudes. **That agreement was not arranged
and it is the strongest available consistency check on the two flight conditions.**

The Kantrowitz self-starting contraction limit rises only from 1.60 to 1 at Mach 7 to 1.63 to 1 at Mach
10, which is why a fixed-geometry inlet is tractable across this range.

The gain factors of 2.51, 2.00 and 1.26 correspond to the published margins of 8, 6 and under 2
decibels, and the loss of 83 percent of the available overshoot follows from them.

The interval from first anomaly to structural overload is 2.00 seconds, which at 2.5 hertz is five
cycles.

The research vehicle is 7.2 percent of stack mass and 24 percent of stack length.

Leading edge stagnation heating at a three millimetre radius is 4.06 and 8.29 megawatts per square
metre at the two conditions, a ratio of 2.04, computed from the Sutton and Graves correlation.

Eleven seconds of powered flight covers 23 kilometres on the second flight and 32 on the third.

A net axial force of 30 to 150 pounds corresponds to accelerations of 0.01 to 0.05 g on a 3,000 pound
vehicle.

### Analysis

**These are engineering conclusions drawn in this article from the relations shown.**

Supersonic combustion is required at the upper end of this range because subsonic-combustion inlet
conditions place the air near or above dissociation before fuel is added, so the alternative destroys
the working fluid rather than merely wasting energy.

A near-constant dynamic pressure corridor follows from the competition between capture mass flow, which
wants density, and structural and thermal load, which limits it.

The thrust-drag margin is a small difference between large numbers, so ground testing and computation
cannot settle its sign when their uncertainty bands are comparable to the difference.

**The gain margin failure and the thrust-drag closure are the same epistemic problem.** Both are small
differences between large quantities, both were predicted rather than measured, and the programme's
value lies in having measured one of them.

Leading edge heating roughly doubles between the two flight conditions at essentially equal dynamic
pressure, because velocity enters cubed and density under a square root.

### Inference

**These are reasoned conclusions the record permits but does not state.**

**The carrier aircraft weight limit is a proximate cause of the first flight's loss.** The board states
that the trajectory was chosen for B-52 weight limits and that the control system was deficient for the
trajectory flown. Joining those two statements is an inference this article makes and the board does
not make in those words.

**The two vehicles flown in 2004 were not identical.** The heating analysis gives a factor of two
between the conditions, and the programme is known to have changed the leading edges for the Mach 10
flight. The precise differences are not reconstructed here.

**The engine burn is taken as approximately eleven seconds on both powered flights.** Reported figures
vary between about ten and about eleven seconds and the distinction does not affect any conclusion
here.

### What the Record Does Not Settle

**The measured value of net thrust is not reconstructed in this article.** The flight established the
sign and the programme's own reconstruction established magnitudes, but reproducing those magnitudes
requires the force accounting the flight papers perform and this article does not repeat.

**Whether the corrected launch vehicle models would have been adequate for a different trajectory is
not established.** The board addressed the trajectory flown.

**No nomenclature reference for the X-43 designation was located.** The two preceding articles in this
series checked their designations against a standard reference and this one could not, so the statement
that the pairing is undisputed rests on the uniform usage of every source consulted rather than on a
register. **That is weaker evidence than it looks**, and it is recorded here rather than glossed.

**The dynamic pressure figure of approximately 1,000 pounds per square foot is computed here from
altitude and Mach number**, using the standard atmosphere rather than measured atmospheric conditions
on the days of the flights. Real conditions differ from the standard atmosphere and the agreement
between the two flights should be read as a consistency check rather than as a measurement.

### On Information Postdating the Editorial Date

This article is written from current knowledge, and the contemporary survey below includes work
published after the editorial date because the directive for this series is a survey of the current
literature rather than a reconstruction of what was knowable in 2025.

## Out of Scope

**The National Aero-Space Plane** is treated only as the programme whose cancellation set the
conditions for this one. Its propulsion work, its politics and its cost are not covered.

**The X-51A Waverider** is named as the successor and treated in its own article later in this series.

**Hydrocarbon scramjet fuels** are outside this article, which treats a hydrogen vehicle. The
endothermic fuel cooling that a hydrocarbon engine requires is a different design problem.

**Detailed combustor chemistry** is taken as given. Ignition delay, mixing and flameholding are named
where they bear on the argument and are not developed.

**The force accounting methodology** used to reconstruct installed thrust from flight data is surveyed
and not reproduced, although it is the technical heart of the programme's own reporting.

**Hypersonic weapons policy** is out of scope entirely.

## Conclusion

**The X-43A was built to find out whether a number was positive, and it found out twice.**

The number is the difference between the thrust an airframe-integrated scramjet produces and the drag
the airframe suffers, and before 27 March 2004 nobody knew its sign in free flight, because both terms
are large, the difference is small, and the uncertainty on each term was comparable to the difference.
**The second flight accelerated and the third held speed**, which places the margin at positive at Mach
7 and approximately zero at Mach 9.6. **That is a more useful pair of results than a speed record**,
because it locates where the closure fails rather than merely showing that it can succeed.

**The first flight was destroyed by the same kind of number and the programme's own investigation said
so plainly.** A roll axis gain margin predicted at 8 decibels against a requirement of 6 became under 2
decibels once the models were corrected, and remained nominally stable even then. **The mishap
reproduced only when every modelling inaccuracy was combined with its uncertainty.** There was no
broken part and no single error large enough to matter, and that is precisely what makes it worth
recording. **A margin is not a quantity. It is a quantity with an uncertainty, and this one had an
uncertainty larger than itself.**

**The programme's stated product was calibrated tools rather than a vehicle**, and by that measure it
succeeded, since engine thrust came in close to prediction on both powered flights and hypersonic
air-breathing design has been anchored to that data since. **The vehicle led nowhere directly.** The
X-43C was cancelled, no operational air-breathing hypersonic aircraft followed, and the eleven seconds
of powered flight remain the extent of what this configuration ever did.

**What survives is a calibration and a caution, and the caution may outlast the calibration.** The
engine data belongs to hydrogen scramjets at Mach 7 and 10. **The finding that a positive margin with
an uncertainty larger than itself is indistinguishable from a negative one belongs to everything.**
